Tanzania. A large East African nation formed in nineteen sixty-four from the merger of Tanganyika and Zanzibar, encompassing diverse landscapes from Mount Kilimanjaro to the Serengeti and serving as home to over one hundred twenty ethnic groups and languages. As a major center of human prehistory and as the site of significant post-colonial nation-building under Julius Nyerere, Tanzania represents both ancient human heritage and modern African independence.

Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest mountain at five thousand eight hundred ninety-five meters, is located in northeastern Tanzania. It is a dormant volcano and iconic symbol of the continent, attracting thousands of climbers annually. The Serengeti is a vast savanna ecosystem in northern Tanzania renowned for its annual migration of wildebeest, zebras, and gazelles—one of the world's most spectacular natural phenomena—and for its diverse megafauna including lions, leopards, and African wild dogs. Lake Victoria, the world's second-largest freshwater lake, is shared by Tanzania, Uganda, and Kenya. It is the source of the Nile River and supports millions of people through fisheries and agriculture.

The Olduvai Gorge, located in northern Tanzania, is one of the most important paleontological sites in the world. Fossil discoveries there by Louis and Mary Leakey provided crucial evidence of human evolution and early hominid species. Tanzania was colonized by Germany in the late nineteenth century, then partitioned between Britain and Belgium after World War One. The British mandate territory of Tanganyika gained independence in nineteen sixty-one, while Zanzibar, an Arab sultanate and British protectorate, gained independence in nineteen sixty-four and shortly after merged with Tanganyika to form Tanzania.

Julius Nyerere, Tanzania's first president from nineteen sixty-four to nineteen eighty-five, pioneered the ideology of Ujamaa, or African socialism, and attempted to build a unified, non-aligned nation free from Cold War pressures. He remains a significant figure in post-colonial African political thought. Dar es Salaam, Tanzania's largest city, is a major port on the Indian Ocean and historical hub of East African trade. The capital was relocated to Dodoma in the nineteen seventies as part of Nyerere's nation-building efforts. Tanzania is ethnically and linguistically diverse, with Swahili as the national language and over one hundred twenty ethnic groups including the Masai, Arusha, and Sukuma maintaining distinct cultures and traditions.
